title: Dynamic queue length mgpu latency sweep
content:
Summary:

Short: We ran an experimental sweep varying the runtime's outbound queue length and NIC/host staging parameters to understand tail-latency behavior on multi-GPU LLM inference (13B class test model). The goal was to find whether adaptive queue sizing (based on request shape and observed link utilization) can reduce p95/p99 spikes without sacrificing throughput.

Key finding (TL;DR):
- Small steady queues (<= 8 outstanding ops per-GPU) give lowest median but exhibit high p99 under peaky bursts.
- Large queues (>= 64) improve p99 for sustained high throughput but increase median latency and cause periodic PCIe read-amplification spikes on some hosts.
- A hybrid, dynamic queue-length controller (warm fast-path small queue, expand on sustained load) reduced p99 by ~25% vs fixed medium queue in our tests.

Experiment setup:
- HW: 8x A100-80GB per-node, NVLink mesh with 2:1 host PCIe Gen4 lines. 2 nodes used for cross-node tests (rdma enabled).
- OS/Driver: Ubuntu 22.04, NVIDIA driver 535.xx, Mellanox OFED.
- Model: internal 13B float16 LLM (sharded TP=2, PP=2, replicated x4). Context L=512, typical prompt len 64 tokens.
- Runtime: current dev branch with queue_length tunable and host-staging toggles (PR 2324).
- Workload: synthetic traffic shaped to emulate PLG taily bursts: poisson arrivals with superimposed 500 qps bursts every 30s, batching allowed up to 8.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency for token-streaming completion, overall throughput (tokens/sec), GPU util, NIC bandwidth, PCIe read/write counters, interrupt rates.
- Tools: nvprof/nsys for per-GPU timelines, ib_read_bw/ib_write_bw for stress, nstat/ethtool for NIC counters, sar/iostat for host IO, perf for interrupts.

Hypotheses we wanted to test:
1) Increasing allowed outstanding ops per-GPU reduces interconnect congestion by amortizing network efficiency (bigger RPCs), but risks larger queuing delays on host-to-device paths (PCIe reads).
2) Bursty traffic exposes a mismatch between runtime queueing and NIC interrupt coalescing, leading to transient stalls.
3) Cross-node RDMA improves throughput but can worsen p99 if host read amplification occurs.

Sweep parameters:
- queue_length per-GPU: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]
- host_staging: [pinned-heap, pinned-page, dma-buf]
- nic_coalesce_us: [0, 64, 200]
- batch_size cap: [1, 4, 8]
- cross-node: local-only vs 2-node RDMA enabled

Representative commands used:
- start harness: ./bench/generate_traffic --qps 200 --burst 500 --shape prompt_len=64 --batch-cap=8
- runtime profiling: ./runtime --queue_length=16 --host_staging=pinned-page --enable-rdma
- nvprof: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output queue16.nsys "./runtime-client --run-bench"
- NIC stress: ib_write_bw -F -D 30 -r 4096 <peer>

Results (selected highlights):
- Fixed queue=4, pinned-heap, nic_coalesce=64: p50=9ms, p95=45ms, p99=130ms, throughput=420k tokens/s
- Fixed queue=32, pinned-heap, nic_coalesce=64: p50=15ms, p95=36ms, p99=80ms, throughput=460k tokens/s but saw PCIe read bursts coinciding with p99 spikes
- Fixed queue=128, dma-buf, nic_coalesce=0: p50=22ms, p95=48ms, p99=95ms, throughput=470k tokens/s, higher host CPU usage and PCIe stalls observed
- Dynamic controller (start=4, expand-to-48 over 2s under sustained 200 qps): p50=11ms, p95=30ms, p99=60ms, throughput=455k tokens/s, far fewer long-tail events

Observations and traces:
- NVTX timelines show long idle gaps on some GPUs immediately before long-tail responses; these map to host-side DMA reads that take multiple ms when PCIe is contended.
- nstat + perf: p99 events aligned with NIC interrupt bursts when coalescing was disabled; coalesce=64us smoothed interrupts and reduced CPU spiking but sometimes delayed small packets resulting in slightly higher p50.
- RDMA cross-node tests improved steady throughput but amplified p99 when combined with large queue_length; hypothesis: more in-flight RDMA windows increase host memory pressure and PCIe activity.
- dma-buf mode reduced host copy overhead but introduced a driver-level serialization point (confirmed by stack traces in perf) that made small-batch median worse.

Practical implications for runtime design:
1) Don't use a single fixed queue length. Different workloads (short prompt vs long completion, small batch vs large batch) benefit from different targets.
2) Implement a conservative initial queue (e.g., 2-8) per-GPU for cold/short requests and allow growth on sustained throughput with a bounded cap. Growth should be rate-limited to avoid triggering PCIe read storms.
3) Add host-level signals to the controller: PCIe read latency percentile, NIC TX queue depth and coalescing counters, and host CPU interrupt load. Use these as backpressure inputs.
4) Expose a NIC-friendly mode that tweaks dev/driver coalescing and toggles dma-buf/pinned strategies depending on batch size heuristics.

Open issues / anomalies:
- On node B (different BIOS/IO config) we saw much worse read amplification for queue>=64. Need firmware/BIOS parity check.
- Some p99 traces show a 6–8ms gap with no GPU activity but steady NIC TX; unclear whether it's net serialization or driver-blocking in userland. Follow-up: collect driver stack traces at p99 using perf and collect kernel slab stats.
- The dynamic controller still has corner cases where it overshoots during sub-second microbursts and then contracts too slowly, causing a brief tail. Need faster contraction heuristics tied to per-request latency signals.

Next steps / action items:
- Diego: run firmware/BIOS parity tests and publish differences (JIRA-2187) — due 2025-10-08.
- Arjun: instrument runtime to surface PCIe read latency percentiles and NIC coalescing counters to the controller (PR 2324 review).
- Samira: reproduce the worst-case p99 with an isolated kernel trace (perf + ftrace) and attach to CONFLUENCE-3342.
- Implement a conservative dynamic controller prototype in runtime (prototype branch queue-adaptive-2025) and run A/B on canary pods next week.

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Try combining dynamic queue with lightweight opportunistic KV-cache prefetching (only prefetch when queue growth < 8).
- Consider a per-link budget allocator: when NVLink/PCIe per-GPU budget saturated, throttle logical queues from replica side.
- Evaluate on 4xA100 vs 8x to see topology sensitivity.

- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2324
- Follow-up ticket: JIRA-2187
